The Egyptian vulture Neophron percnopterus exhibits reproductive parameters that reflect a relatively slow life history strategy typical of long-lived accipitrids. Field studies in the Canary Islands have recorded females typically producing a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], with each clutch containing two eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing two eggs], a modest output that correlates with extended parental investment. When incubating eggs at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the development period requires approximately 42 days [ab = approximately 42 days], a duration comparable to that observed in other medium-sized Old World vultures. The weight of freshly laid eggs averages around 220 grams, though newly hatched nestlings weigh considerably less, at approximately 150 grams [Wwb = approximately 150 grams], reflecting the substantial yolk reserves consumed during the lengthy incubation phase. This disparity between egg mass and hatchling mass underscores the energetic cost of embryonic development under stable thermal conditions.

Among captive populations maintained at an ambient temperature of approximately 40 °C [T = 40 °C], several key developmental milestones have been documented with notable consistency. Fledging, defined as the first successful achievement of sustained flight, occurs at roughly 75 days after hatching [tx = roughly 75 days after hatching], though some observers have reported a range extending from 70 to 85 days depending on food availability and individual condition at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. The chick progresses through a conspicuous pin-feathered nestling stage before achieving full flight feather maturation. Biparental provisioning continues beyond this point, gradually diminishing as the juvenile bird refines its foraging skills. The transition from complete dependence on parental care to independent foraging represents a critical period of high mortality risk, one that shapes the species overall demographic trajectory and sets the stage for later reproductive maturation.

Sexual maturation in the Egyptian vulture is a protracted process relative to many other avian scavengers of similar body mass. Under typical thermal conditions of approximately 40 °C [T = 40 °C], puberty is attained at a mean age of 225 days after hatching [tp = 225 days after hatching], although some sources document an earlier window of 70 to 85 days for the initial onset of gonadal activity. This discrepancy likely reflects variation in nutritional regimes across study populations. The attainment of full reproductive maturity, however, occurs much later, with the first successful breeding event typically recorded at approximately four years after hatching [tR = approximately four years after hatching] at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This delayed reproduction is consistent with the species extended period of somatic growth and the time required to secure a breeding territory. The ultimate body masses attained by adult individuals show meaningful variability between populations.

Adult body mass represents a key indicator of individual condition and correlates with reproductive success in many raptors. For Egyptian vultures, asymptotic body mass in wild populations has been recorded at 2026 grams [Wwi = 2026 grams] for individuals in prime condition from the Ethiopian highlands, a value that reflects the upper limits of the species size range across its extensive distribution. A slightly lower ultimate weight of 1928 grams [Wwi = 1928 grams] has been documented in European breeding populations of the subspecies Neophron percnopterus percnopterus, suggesting a latitudinal gradient in body size consistent with Bergmanns rule. This modest degree of sexual dimorphism, with females typically weighing marginally more than males, is characteristic of many accipitrid species and likely relates to the energetic demands of egg production and incubation.

Longevity records for the Egyptian vulture, based on both wild populations and captive individuals, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 37 years [am = approximately 37 years] under controlled conditions maintained at approximately 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This remarkable lifespan, among the longest documented for any Accipitridae species of comparable body size, reflects the vultures exceptionally low adult mortality rate once individuals have survived the high-risk juvenile period. Wild populations, however, seldom achieve this potential due to anthropogenic threats including poisoning, electrocution, and habitat degradation. This low intrinsic rate of increase renders the species particularly vulnerable to any increase in adult mortality, a demographic reality that conservation programs must address.
